title: Linear-length witnesses for reachability in each fixed vector addition system
formal: For every integer \(d\geq1\) and finite set \(V\subseteq\mathbb Z^d\), does there exist a constant \(C_V\geq1\) such that every reachable pair \(s,t\in\mathbb N^d\) has a run of length at most \(C_V(\|s\|_1+\|t\|_1)\)?
why: The conjecture isolates whether unbounded shortest-run growth is caused by changing the transition system or can already occur within one fixed system. This structural distinction is fundamental for understanding the complexity of reachability when only numerical configurations vary.
status_note: The 2022 source and 2024 fixed-VASS paper retain the linear shortest-run conjecture. A bounded later-work check on 13 September 2026 did not locate a proof or a fixed-system counterexample. The zero-endpoint inequality convention is an explicit editorial repair of the literal strict source wording, not a claimed research resolution.

progress.text: Jecker poses the system-dependent linear shortest-run conjecture.
Draghici, Haase and Ryzhikov establish fixed-VASS lower bounds, explain the conjecture’s PSPACE consequence with binary endpoints, and report no counterevidence from their constructions.

sentences: A fixed vector addition system supplies a finite collection of updates on nonnegative integer vectors.
The conjecture asks whether every reachable pair has a run linear in the numerical sizes of its endpoints.
The multiplicative constant may depend on the entire fixed system, while the endpoints vary freely.
The non-strict bound includes the zero-length run from zero to itself.
This structural witness bound would have complexity consequences, but it is not a linear-time algorithm in binary input length.

definitions: A vector addition system (VAS) is the finite set \(V\) of allowed displacement vectors; there is no control-state graph. Its configurations are vectors in \(\mathbb N^d\), where zero coordinates are allowed. A run from \(s\) to \(t\) is a finite sequence \(c_0=s,c_1,\ldots,c_m=t\) with \(c_i\in\mathbb N^d\) and \(c_i-c_{i-1}\in V\) for all \(1\leq i\leq m\). Its length is the number \(m\) of transitions, not the magnitude of its largest counter. Empty runs of length zero are permitted, so every configuration reaches itself. The norm is \(\|x\|_1=\sum_{j=1}^d |x_j|\). The whole system, including its dimension, number of updates and their integer magnitudes, is fixed before \(C_V\) is chosen. The constant must then work for all source and target vectors in that system. There are no tests except the requirement that updated coordinates remain nonnegative. No algorithm for computing \(C_V\), finding a short run or deciding reachability in a specified time is required. The bound measures numerical endpoint magnitudes, not their binary encoding lengths. Choosing another fixed norm would change only the system-dependent constant. The non-strict inequality includes the zero-to-zero empty run; the source’s strict wording otherwise has an artificial zero-endpoint exception. For positive endpoint norm sums, strict and non-strict versions are equivalent after enlarging \(C_V\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal system-dependent linear witness bound. Alternatively give one explicit finite VAS \(V\) and prove in Lean that for every \(C\geq1\) there are reachable endpoints \(s,t\) for which every run has length greater than \(C(\|s\|_1+\|t\|_1)\). Letting the update system vary with \(C\), using binary bit length instead of endpoint magnitudes, or merely displaying one unnecessarily long run does not refute the proposition.

context_blocks.text: For a one-counter system allowing increments and decrements by one, the shortest run has length \(|s-t|\), which meets the desired bound. The conjecture says that more involved interactions among a fixed finite collection of counters never force a superlinear shortest detour as the endpoints grow.

Jecker’s source formulates a short-witness conjecture, despite the entry’s broad complexity title. The present title and criterion expose that actual mathematical claim. The choice of a non-strict bound simply handles the permitted empty run at zero rather than turning a wording defect into a counterexample.

A fixed system can contain very large displacement constants, and the allowed multiplicative constant may be correspondingly large. Exhibiting a family of larger and larger systems with hard instances would not disprove this conjecture: a counterexample must keep one finite update set for every endpoint pair.

The 2024 fixed-VASS paper discusses Jecker’s conjecture and reports that its lower-bound constructions give no evidence against it. It proves PSPACE-hardness for a fixed five-counter VASS when initial counter values are binary and explains the PSPACE upper-bound implication of the proposed short-path property.

There is no conflict between a path linear in endpoint magnitudes and a high complexity measured in binary digits. A counter value with a short binary encoding can be exponentially larger than that encoding, so writing out such a path may already take exponentially many steps.

A positive answer would constrain how much of the infinite configuration graph is needed to witness each reachable pair once the system is fixed. It would not make all VAS reachability uniformly linear-time, since the constant carries the entire fixed system and the target is existential.
